headings.title: Anatomy and Structure of the Heart
headings.content:
The human heart is a hollow, muscular organ roughly the size of a clenched fist, situated centrally in the thoracic cavity within the mediastinum. It is enclosed by the **pericardium**, a double-walled sac that protects the organ and prevents overfilling with blood. The heart wall consists of three distinct layers:

- **Epicardium**: The thin, transparent outer layer forming the visceral pericardium.
- **Myocardium**: The thick middle layer composed of specialized cardiac muscle tissue responsible for pumping blood.
- **Endocardium**: The smooth inner lining of chambers and valves that reduces friction as blood flows through.

Internally, the heart is divided into four chambers: two upper **atria** (receiving chambers) and two lower **ventricles** (pumping chambers). A thick muscular wall called the **septum** separates the left and right sides, preventing the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Blood flow is strictly one-way, controlled by four valves. The **atrioventricular (AV) valves**—the tricuspid on the right and the mitral (bicuspid) on the left—separate atria from ventricles. The **semilunar valves**—the aortic and pulmonary valves—guard the exits from the ventricles into the major arteries.

headings.title: Functions of the Heart
headings.content:
The primary function of the heart is to maintain adequate circulation of blood through the pulmonary and systemic circuits, ensuring every tissue receives oxygen and nutrients while metabolic waste products are removed. 

1. **Pulmonary Circulation**: The right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood received from the body into the lungs via the pulmonary artery, where carbon dioxide is exchanged for oxygen.
2. **Systemic Circulation**: The left side of the heart receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it out through the aorta to supply the entire body.
3. **Endocrine Function**: Specialized myocardial cells in the atria secrete **atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)**, a hormone that helps regulate blood pressure by promoting sodium excretion by the kidneys.
4. **Pressure Generation**: The rhythmic contraction of the heart creates the hydrostatic pressure necessary to push blood through miles of blood vessels.

headings.title: Cardiac Cycle and Heart Sounds
headings.content:
The **cardiac cycle** describes the sequence of events in a single heartbeat, encompassing periods of contraction (**systole**) and relaxation (**diastole**). It operates in a coordinated rhythm to fill and empty the chambers efficiently.

During atrial diastole and ventricular filling, blood flows passively into the heart chambers, followed by atrial systole which tops off the ventricles. Next, ventricular systole begins; rising pressure forces the AV valves shut, creating the first heart sound, **S1** (the "lub" sound). As ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aorta and pulmonary trunk, the semilunar valves open to eject blood. Once ejection concludes, ventricular relaxation drops internal pressure below arterial pressure, snapping the semilunar valves shut and producing the second heart sound, **S2** (the "dub" sound).

Normal heart sounds are caused by the turbulence of blood when valve leaflets snap shut, not by the muscular contraction itself. Abnormal turbulent flow across damaged valves produces extra sounds known as murmurs.

headings.title: Conducting System of the Heart
headings.content:
The heart possesses the unique property of **autorhythmicity**, meaning it can generate its own electrical impulses without external nervous system stimulation. This is managed by specialized pacemaker and conduction tissues.

- **Sinoatrial (SA) Node**: Located in the right atrial wall, it is the primary pacemaker that sets the normal sinus rhythm.
- **Atrioventricular (AV) Node**: Situated at the junction of the atria and ventricles, it briefly delays the impulse to allow complete ventricular filling.
- **Bundle of His (AV Bundle)**: Transmits the electrical signal from the AV node down into the interventricular septum.
- **Bundle Branches**: Divide into right and left pathways to carry the impulse toward the apex of the heart.
- **Purkinje Fibers**: Spread rapidly through the ventricular myocardium, ensuring synchronized contraction from the bottom up.

Disruption in any part of this pathway leads to **arrhythmias**, where the heart beats too fast, too slow, or irregularly.

headings.title: Electrocardiography (ECG)
headings.content:
An **electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG)** is a non-invasive diagnostic tool that records the electrical activity of the heart over time using electrodes placed on the skin. A standard ECG tracing displays characteristic waveforms representing specific electrical events.

- **P wave**: Represents atrial depolarization, the electrical spread through the atria preceding their contraction.
- **QRS complex**: Represents ventricular depolarization, the massive electrical spread through the thick ventricles. Atrial repolarization is also hidden within this wave.
- **T wave**: Represents ventricular repolarization, the recovery phase where ventricles return to their resting electrical state.

Clinicians analyze the size, shape, and time intervals between these waves to diagnose myocardial infarctions, electrolyte imbalances, and conduction blocks.
